newsitem.title: USA: Political worries push dollar to 42-month high vs. yen.
newsitem.headline: Political worries push dollar to 42-month high vs. yen.

text.p: The dollar Monday climbed to its highest level in 3-1/2 years against the Japanese yen, which continued to suffer from Japan's indecisive general election on Oct. 20.
But the dollar's rise against the yen did not translate into gains against other major currencies.
The yen's slide also bolstered the Swiss franc while the British pound and German mark reached their highest levels since February 1993 against the Japanese currency.
The yen fell again as Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto continued to struggle to stitch together a government more than a week after the election.

While Japan's dominant Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) won the most seats in the lower house of parliament, it fell short of capturing a majority and has failed to find a partner to form a new coalition government.

Most politicians and analysts now expect Hashimoto to head into a new session of parliament at the head of a minority government, making another election a constant threat and forcing investors who crave political stability to pull their money out of yen-based assets and put it to work elsewhere.
"People are variously attributing it to a lack of a political settlement in Japan," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan, in New York.
"There are still ongoing negotiations to form a coalition and a lack of progress on that front is seen as the main factor undermining the yen," Pettit said.
The dollar rose to 114.38 yen on Monday -- its highest since April 1993, when it reached 115.20 -- before settling at 114.21 yen in U.S. trading, up from 113.42 late Friday.
The advance picked up steam early Monday when the dollar hurdled 113.60 yen, what traders call a key resistance level that was nearly retested during last week's rally.
Low Japanese interest rates also fuelled the move out of yen-based assets into investments based in dollars and other major currencies, traders said.
The political stalemate is compounding the yen's problems by diminishing the odds that Tokyo's current policy of holding interest rates at record low levels will soon be altered.
"It's the concept of the hung parliament and ... that interest rates are going to remain low there," said Tim Summerfield, senior foreign exchange trader at Bank of Boston.
The strength of the European currencies against the yen took a slight toll on the dollar, traders said.
"It is really not the dollar that's trading at all, said John Nelson, senior vice president at ABN-AMRO Bank in Chicago. "It is just the yen being weak against a whole host of currencies."
The dollar fell to 1.5190 marks late in New York from 1.5200 late on Friday, and to 1.2611 Swiss francs from 1.2617.
The pound rose to $1.6128 from $1.6048 on Friday.
The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3445 from C$1.3449.
